name: Early forays into the Levant
what: Small groups crossed from north-east Africa to the Levant about 190,000 years ago (Misliya), and again about 120,000 years ago (Skhul and Qafzeh).
why: These early movers did not leave lasting descendants that geneticists can find; the climate turned and the Levant went back to Neanderthals.

sources.cite: Hershkovitz, I. et al., "The earliest modern humans outside Africa", Science 359, 456-459 (2018)
Valladas, H. et al., "Thermoluminescence dating of Mousterian Proto-Cro-Magnon remains from Israel and the origin of modern man", Nature 331, 614-616 (1988)
Grün, R. et al., "U-series and ESR analyses of bones and teeth relating to the human burials from Skhul", Journal of Human Evolution 49, 316-334 (2005)

name: Out of Africa by the southern route
what: The ancestors of everyone outside Africa crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb, then moved along the coasts of Arabia and India to Sunda and Sahul.
why: Genomes put the main dispersal at 60,000 to 50,000 years ago; Madjedbebe in Australia may be older, which is still argued.

sources.cite: Clarkson, C. et al., "Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago", Nature 547, 306-310 (2017)
O'Connell, J. F. et al., "When did Homo sapiens first reach Southeast Asia and Sahul?", PNAS 115, 8482-8490 (2018)
Oktaviana, A. A. et al., "Narrative cave art in Indonesia by 51,200 years ago", Nature 631, 814-818 (2024)

name: Into Europe
what: From the Levant through Anatolia and up the Danube: modern humans were across Europe by 42,000 years ago.
why: They met Neanderthals along the way; within a few thousand years only one kind of human was left.

sources.cite: Slimak, L. et al., "Modern human incursion into Neanderthal territories 54,000 years ago at Mandrin, France", Science Advances 8, eabj9496 (2022)
Hublin, J.-J. et al., "Initial Upper Palaeolithic Homo sapiens from Bacho Kiro Cave, Bulgaria", Nature 581, 299-302 (2020)
Mylopotamitaki, D. et al., "Homo sapiens reached the higher latitudes of Europe by 45,000 years ago", Nature 626, 341-346 (2024)

name: Into Siberia and the Arctic
what: North across Central Asia to western Siberia (Ust'-Ishim), Lake Baikal, and the Arctic coast at Yana.
why: These northern people later met East Asians; their mixed descendants crossed Beringia.

sources.cite: Fu, Q. et al., "Genome sequence of a 45,000-year-old modern human from western Siberia", Nature 514, 445-449 (2014)
Pitulko, V. V. et al., "The Yana RHS site: humans in the Arctic before the Last Glacial Maximum", Science 303, 52-56 (2004)
Raghavan, M. et al., "Upper Palaeolithic Siberian genome reveals dual ancestry of Native Americans", Nature 505, 87-91 (2014)

name: Into East Asia and Japan
what: From mainland Southeast Asia north through China; by 38,000 years ago people had crossed to Japan.
why: Tianyuan shows East Asian ancestry was in place 40,000 years ago.

sources.cite: Freidline, S. E. et al., "Early presence of Homo sapiens in Southeast Asia by 86-68 kyr at Tam Pà Ling, Northern Laos", Nature Communications 14, 3193 (2023)
Fu, Q. et al., "DNA analysis of an early modern human from Tianyuan Cave, China", PNAS 110, 2223-2227 (2013)

name: Into the Americas along the coast
what: People waited in Beringia during the Last Glacial Maximum, then moved south along a coast of kelp forests as the Cordilleran ice pulled back.
why: Monte Verde in Chile was lived in 14,500 years ago; White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, mean some came even before the ice peaked.

sources.cite: Dillehay, T. D. et al., "Monte Verde: seaweed, food, medicine, and the peopling of South America", Science 320, 784-786 (2008)
Gilbert, M. T. P. et al., "DNA from pre-Clovis human coprolites in Oregon, North America", Science 320, 786-789 (2008)
Bennett, M. R. et al., "Evidence of humans in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum", Science 373, 1528-1531 (2021)

name: Down the ice-free corridor
what: A passage opened between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice about 13,800 years ago; Clovis hunters spread across the plains soon after.
why: The corridor came too late to be the first way in, but it linked Alaska and the plains.

sources.cite: Waters, M. R. & Stafford, T. W., "Redefining the age of Clovis: implications for the peopling of the Americas", Science 315, 1122-1126 (2007)

name: Across the Bassian land bridge to Tasmania
what: With the sea 60 m or more lower, Tasmania was a peninsula; people walked there about 40,000 years ago.
why: When the strait flooded about 14,000 years ago, Tasmanians were cut off for 10,000 years.

sources.cite: Lambeck, K. & Chappell, J., "Sea level change through the last glacial cycle", Science 292, 679-686 (2001)
